input_signals.name: Self-funded deleveraging under leverage stress
input_signals.expression: MUL(MUL(RATIO(SUB(dltr, dltis), at), INDICATOR(RATIO(oancf, at), 0)), INDICATOR(RATIO(lt, at), 0.65))
input_signals.hypothesis: Net long-term debt retirement financed by positive operating cash flow at highly levered firms reveals a credible balance-sheet repair path and declining default probability, which is priced with a lag.
input_signals.reasoning: The double indicator restricts the repayment signal to firms that are both levered (lt/at above 0.65) and internally cash-generating, distinguishing voluntary deleveraging from distressed asset-sale repayment. Unlike a pure repayment signal, the mechanism requires the joint state of high liabilities and positive internal funding, so it captures recovery quality rather than debt flow per se.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( mul( ratio( sub( dltr, dltis ), at ), indicator( ratio( oancf, at ), 0 ) ), indicator( ratio( lt, at ), 0.65 ) )

input_signals.name: Chronic-loss financing dependence
input_signals.expression: MUL(RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(ADD(prstkc, dltr), dvt)), at), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(NEG(ib), 0), 3))
input_signals.hypothesis: Net external financing raised by firms with a persistent multi-year loss record measures dependence on capital markets for survival; the longer the loss streak, the more each dollar raised reflects deferred failure rather than expansion, predicting negative abnormal returns.
input_signals.reasoning: The financing leg is a full net-external-finance flow (issuance minus repayments, buybacks and dividends), while the distress leg is a persistence count of loss years over three years, so the signal scales with both the amount and the chronicity of dependence. A single bad year earns weight 1 and a three-year loss streak weight 3, encoding the economic idea that repeated recourse to external funding by chronic losers is progressively worse news.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ratio( sub( add( sstk, dltis ), add( add( prstkc, dltr ), dvt ) ), at ), ts_sum( indicator( neg( ib ), 0 ), 3 ) )

input_signals.name: Continuous coverage-weighted deleveraging
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(dltr, dltis), at), 2), MUL(RANK(RATIO(lt, at)), RANK(RATIO(oancf, lt))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Net long-term debt retirement is good news in proportion to how levered the firm is and how well operating cash flow covers its liabilities: high-coverage, high-leverage repayers are genuinely repairing solvency, while the same repayment by an unlevered firm is uninformative.
input_signals.reasoning: The gen-0 conditional version produced FMB t=+3.1 but only 2% alpha because two hard indicators set the signal to exactly zero for most firms, leaving a thin and unstable long leg. Replacing the 0.65 leverage cutoff and the sign indicator with a product of continuous leverage and cash-flow-coverage ranks preserves the identical economic state (levered but internally funded deleveraging) while giving every firm a graded weight, which should widen the sorted spread without diluting the mechanism.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ratio( sub( dltr, dltis ), at ), 2 ), mul( rank( ratio( lt, at ) ), rank( ratio( oancf, lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Serial dilution with chronic cash shortfall
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), at)), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(oancf, lct))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Repeated recourse to the equity market across several years, in a firm whose cash and operating cash flow are both small relative to current liabilities, identifies a business that survives only by serial dilution; the market underestimates the cumulative cost of this dependence.
input_signals.reasoning: Single-year issuance conflates a one-off opportunistic offering with a habitual funding model, and the archive has only tested one-year flows on the equity side; cumulating three years of sstk shifts the concept from an event to a regime. The distress weight also switches to two flow-versus-current-liability coverage measures, so both legs describe chronic states rather than annual shocks, which should reduce turnover and stabilize the portfolio.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ts_sum( sstk, 3 ), at ) ), sumrank( neg( ratio( che, lct ) ), neg( ratio( oancf, lct ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Burn rate against post-issuance resources
input_signals.hypothesis: For a firm consuming cash in operations, the relevant distress measure is how fast it burns relative to the resources it actually has after this year's fundraising: a high burn-to-resources ratio means the runway is short and another dilutive raise is imminent, which predicts low returns, whereas a firm that raised many years of burn is not under financing pressure.
input_signals.reasoning: This is not an issuance-magnitude signal at all — equity raised enters the denominator as a resource that relieves pressure, so two firms with identical issuance rank differently depending on their burn, which inverts the direction in which sstk enters relative to the entire archive and to the net-share-issuance anomaly. The indicator confines the measure to cash-burning firms, where the runway concept is economically defined, and the ratio combines a financing flow with two distress variables in a single non-separable quantity rather than a product of a financing leg and a distress weight.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( indicator( neg( oancf ), 0 ), winsor( ratio( abs( oancf ), add( che, sstk ) ), 2 ) )

input_signals.name: Purified dilution-illiquidity interaction
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), at))), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(oancf, lct))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The return penalty is specific to the joint state of repeated equity raising and inability to cover current liabilities; once the issuance leg is centered, the signal is high only for illiquid heavy diluters and low for illiquid firms that do not dilute, so any surviving spread is attributable to the interaction rather than to illiquidity alone.
input_signals.reasoning: Centering the financing rank makes the product a textbook interaction term with zero conditional mean for every moderator level, which removes exactly the distress main effect that gen-4 showed was producing near-identical alphas for four contradictory financing legs. If the mechanism is real this should retain both the slope and a substantial alpha; if the alpha collapses, we will have learned that the entire family was a distress-anomaly repackaging — either outcome is decisive for the remaining generations.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( rank( ratio( ts_sum( sstk, 3 ), at ) ) ), sumrank( neg( ratio( che, lct ) ), neg( ratio( oancf, lct ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Dilution measured against pre-issuance size
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), LAG(at, 3))), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(oancf, lct))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Cumulative issuance divided by current assets understates dependence for the heaviest diluters because the proceeds themselves inflate the denominator; scaling three years of equity raised by the asset base that existed before the raises measures how much the firm has been rebuilt with outside money, which is the economically relevant quantity.
input_signals.reasoning: This is a mechanical bias fix rather than a restatement: a firm that tripled its asset base with equity gets a ratio near 0.7 under current-asset scaling but near 2 under pre-issuance scaling, so the ordering of the most dependent firms changes materially. Because the archive's best joint evidence comes from this leg, sharpening its measurement is the highest-value refinement available, and the moderator is held identical so attribution is unambiguous.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ts_sum( sstk, 3 ), lag( at, 3 ) ) ), sumrank( neg( ratio( che, lct ) ), neg( ratio( oancf, lct ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Serial dilution with an accumulated earnings deficit
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm that keeps selling equity while its retained earnings remain deeply negative has funded a cumulative history of value destruction with outside capital; this stock-of-losses state, rather than current liquidity, may be the distress condition that makes repeated dilution predictive.
input_signals.reasoning: Retained-earnings deficit has only ever been paired with single-year payout or net-debt legs in this archive, never with the multi-year issuance leg that generates the slopes, and unlike liquidity ratios it is a slow-moving cumulative state that should produce low turnover and stable portfolios. It also serves as a moderator-substitution test for signals 1 and 3: if the effect persists across two very different distress states, the mechanism is about dependence on external equity rather than about any single distress proxy.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ts_sum( sstk, 3 ), at ) ), rank( neg( ratio( re, at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Within-deficit-group dilution contrast
input_signals.hypothesis: Among firms whose current liabilities already exceed their current assets, heavy serial diluters should underperform their non-diluting peers in the same working-capital-deficit condition, while firms with positive working capital are simply uninformative for this mechanism.
input_signals.reasoning: Centering the issuance rank before applying the sample gate places untreated (positive working capital) firms at exactly the middle of the cross-section rather than at the bottom, so the long and short extremes are both drawn from the working-capital-deficit group — the genuine within-group contrast the critic showed the previous version failed to deliver. The tie block is now neutral for the Fama-MacBeth slope as well, since the zero values sit at the conditional mean of the regressor.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( rank( ratio( ts_sum( sstk, 3 ), at ) ) ), indicator( neg( ratio( wcap, at ) ), 0 ) )

input_signals.name: Equity raised per dollar of pre-period revenue
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), LAG(sale, 3))), SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), NEG(RATIO(oancf, lct))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Dependence on outside equity is best expressed relative to the operating scale the firm actually runs — a company that has raised two years of revenue from shareholders is living on investor capital regardless of how large its balance sheet has become — and this dependence is priced most sharply when current liabilities cannot be covered.
input_signals.reasoning: Assets are the direct destination of issuance proceeds, so even a lagged asset base is partly endogenous to the financing history, whereas revenue is a genuinely independent measure of operating scale; this makes the denominator choice an economic refinement rather than a rescaling. Sale-based scaling also keeps the deep-burn, pre-revenue diluters at the informative extreme instead of compressing them, which is where the mechanism should be strongest.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ts_sum( sstk, 3 ), lag( sale, 3 ) ) ), sumrank( neg( ratio( che, lct ) ), neg( ratio( oancf, lct ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Equity funding an operating working-capital bloat
input_signals.hypothesis: When a serial equity issuer's non-cash current assets are growing faster than its sales, the money raised is being absorbed by uncollected receivables and unsold inventory rather than by productive investment, which signals deteriorating operations and the likelihood of further dilution.
input_signals.reasoning: Operating working-capital efficiency is an entirely new distress axis for this archive and it is conceptually independent of the funding-capacity ratios that have dominated: it asks where the money went in the operating cycle, not whether obligations can be met. It also gives a specific, testable use-of-proceeds mechanism that the earlier one-year change-in-cash test could not capture, since inventory and receivable bloat is exactly how proceeds disappear without cash ever appearing on the balance sheet.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ts_sum( sstk, 3 ), at ) ), rank( growth( ratio( sub( act, che ), sale ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Serial dilution with near-term debt overhang
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm that has repeatedly sold equity and also carries debt maturing within the year that is large relative to its entire current asset base faces a hard deadline: the next repayment must be met from a new raise, so its bargaining position with investors is at its weakest and returns should be poor.
input_signals.reasoning: Every moderator tested so far measures obligations in aggregate (current liabilities, working capital, cash flow coverage); this one measures the *maturity* of the claim that is about to come due against liquid resources, which is the specific state that forces dilution on the issuer's terms rather than the firm's. Both legs are stable, always-positive ratios with no sign-flip or blow-up risk, and the debt-overhang leg is not a rescaling of anything in the archive, so the test is about a new distress state rather than a new denominator.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ts_sum( sstk, 3 ), at ) ), rank( ratio( dlc, act ) ) )

input_signals.name: Distributions exceeding internal cash generation before maturities
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm that has distributed more cash to shareholders over three years than its operations produced, while carrying near-term maturities large relative to its current assets, has funded shareholder payments from borrowings or reserves and is exposed when the debt must be refinanced.
input_signals.reasoning: Expressing affordability as a signed difference scaled by assets eliminates the sign inversion the critic identified in the ratio version — stressed payers with negative cumulative cash flow now score at the top of the distribution, exactly where the hypothesis places them, instead of flipping to the long side. It is also economically distinct from the evaluated payout-level signal because a large dividend paid out of larger cash flow now scores near zero rather than extreme.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( ts_sum( dvt, 3 ), ts_sum( oancf, 3 ) ), at ) ), rank( ratio( dlc, act ) ) )

input_signals.name: Dilution against a floored survival horizon
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(sstk, 3), at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(che, ADD(ADD(MUL(NEG(oancf), INDICATOR(NEG(oancf), 0)), dlc), dltr)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A market-dependent firm's survival horizon is its cash divided by the cash it must actually spend — its operating burn when it burns, plus maturing and amortizing debt; serial diluters with short horizons must return to the market imminently and underperform.
input_signals.reasoning: The burn term is now floored via MUL(NEG(oancf), INDICATOR(NEG(oancf), 0)), so profitable firms contribute zero burn and are scored by their debt obligations alone, repairing the sign contradiction the critic identified while keeping the denominator strictly non-negative. Including scheduled amortization (dltr) alongside maturing short-term debt both completes the obligation measure economically and reduces the incidence of a zero denominator, and no archive signal has expressed the distress state as a horizon in time units rather than a static ratio.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ts_sum( sstk, 3 ), at ) ), rank( neg( ratio( che, add( add( mul( neg( oancf ), indicator( neg( oancf ), 0 ) ), dlc ), dltr ) ) ) ) )
